title: Statistical Intervals for a Single Sample

blocks.x: An estimate $\hat\theta$ will not equal $\theta$ exactly. A statistical interval says how far off it may be. Three kinds are used.
A confidence interval contains a population parameter (such as $\mu$) with a stated probability, over repeated sampling.
A prediction interval contains a single future observation with a stated probability.
A tolerance interval contains at least a stated proportion of the population, with a stated confidence.
For the same data the three have different widths:
the confidence interval is narrowest. It concerns only the mean, whose uncertainty shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$;
the prediction interval is wider. It must also cover the variability of one new value;
the tolerance interval is widest.

sections.title: Confidence Interval on the Mean of a Normal Distribution, Variance Known

blocks.x: Development of the Confidence Interval and Its Basic Properties
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be a random sample from $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ known and $\mu$ unknown. From Chapter 1,
Z=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\Normal(0,1).

Let $z_{\alpha/2}$ cut off a right-tail area $\alpha/2$ under the standard normal curve. ($z_{0.025}=1.96$, $z_{0.05}=1.645$, $z_{0.005}=2.576$.) Then $\Prob(-z_{\alpha/2}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$. Solve the inequalities for $\mu$:
\Prob\Big(\bar{X}-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\ \le\ \mu\ \le\ \bar{X}+z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\Big)=1-\alpha.

blocks.name: Definition
blocks.title: Confidence interval on the mean, $\sigma$ known

blocks.x: If $\bar{x}$ is the mean of a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with known variance $\sigma^2$, a $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is
\bar{x}-z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\ \le\ \mu\ \le\ \bar{x}+z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}.
$1-\alpha$ is the confidence level. The two endpoints are the lower and upper confidence limits.
Ten measurements of the impact energy of a steel have $\bar{x}=64.46$ J. $\sigma=1$ J is known.
The $95\%$ describes the procedure, not the particular interval.
Before the data are collected, the random interval $\bar{X}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$ contains the fixed $\mu$ with probability $0.95$.

After the data are in, the computed interval either contains $\mu$ or it does not. You cannot say “the probability that $\mu$ lies in $(63.84,65.08)$ is $0.95$”. In the frequentist view $\mu$ is not random.
Correct reading: if you repeated the procedure on many independent samples, about $95\%$ of the intervals would cover $\mu$.

blocks.caption: Ten confidence intervals from ten samples. The vertical line is the true $\mu$; the two intervals that miss it are drawn in orange. Over many samples, $95\%$ of $95\%$ intervals cover $\mu$.

blocks.x: Properties

Width. The length is $2z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$, called the precision. It shrinks with larger $n$ and larger $\alpha$ (lower confidence). It grows with larger $\sigma$ and higher confidence. $E=z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$ is the error (margin of error) in estimating $\mu$ by $\bar{x}$.
Confidence against precision. More confidence costs width. Going from $95\%$ to $99\%$ replaces $1.96$ by $2.576$, a $31\%$ longer interval.
Choice of Sample Size
With confidence $100(1-\alpha)\%$ we are sure the error $\abs{\bar{x}-\mu}$ does not exceed $E=z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$. Solve for $n$:

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Sample size for estimating a mean

blocks.x: To be $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confident that the error in estimating $\mu$ by $\bar{x}$ is at most $E$, use
n=\left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma}{E}\right)^2,\qquad\text{rounded up to the next integer.}
In Example 2.2, how large must $n$ be for a $95\%$ error of at most $0.5$ J? $n=(1.96\cdot1/0.5)^2=15.37$, so $n=16$.
$n$ varies as $1/E^2$. Halving the error multiplies the sample size by four.
One-sided Confidence Bounds

Sometimes only an upper or lower limit matters (a maximum emission level, a minimum strength). The two kinds of statement are built differently. Table 2.2.4 lists both for every parameter in this chapter.
$100(1-\alpha)\%$ upper confidence bound: $\mu\le\bar{x}+z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n$.
$100(1-\alpha)\%$ lower confidence bound: $\bar{x}-z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n\le\mu$.
Note $z_\alpha$, not $z_{\alpha/2}$. All of the error probability $\alpha$ sits in one tail, because only one end is claimed. Each bound alone has coverage $1-\alpha$.
Same data as above.
$95\%$ lower bound: $64.46-1.645/\sqrt{10}=63.94$. Tighter than the two-sided lower limit $63.84=64.46-1.96/\sqrt{10}$.
$95\%$ upper bound: $64.46+0.52=64.98$. The two-sided upper limit is $65.08$.

Two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval: $\alpha/2$ in each tail. The critical value has subscript $\alpha/2$ ($z_{\alpha/2}$, $t_{\alpha/2, u}$, $\chi^2_{\alpha/2, u}$ and $\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2, u}$, $f_{\alpha/2}$ and $f_{1-\alpha/2}$).

One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bound: all of $\alpha$ in one tail. The critical value has subscript $\alpha$ ($z_\alpha$, $t_{\alpha, u}$, $\chi^2_{\alpha, u}$ or $\chi^2_{1-\alpha, u}$, $f_\alpha$ or $f_{1-\alpha}$). Write only one limit. The other side stays open ($-\infty$ or $+\infty$, or $0$/$1$ for a variance or proportion that cannot go further).

They are not the same confidence level. A one-sided $95\%$ upper bound is not the upper end of a two-sided $95\%$ interval. The upper end of a two-sided $95\%$ interval is a one-sided $97.5\%$ bound. The upper end of a two-sided $90\%$ interval is a one-sided $95\%$ bound.

Tests. A one-sided test at level $\alpha$ matches a one-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bound. A two-sided test at level $\alpha$ matches a two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval. Reject $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta>\theta_0$ exactly when the lower bound exceeds $\theta_0$. Reject against $H_1:\theta<\theta_0$ exactly when the upper bound is below $\theta_0$.

blocks.caption: One-sided and two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ limits. In each row the two-sided interval uses both limits with $\alpha/2$, the upper bound uses only the upper limit with $\alpha$, the lower bound only the lower limit with $\alpha$.

blocks.x: Multipliers for a $95\%$ statement:
$t$ with $9$ degrees of freedom: $t_{0.025,9}=2.262$ against $t_{0.05,9}=1.833$.

Sample size follows the same rule. A two-sided interval with error at most $E$ needs $n=(z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/E)^2$. A one-sided bound at distance at most $E$ from $\bar{x}$ needs the smaller $n=(z_\alpha\sigma/E)^2$.
General Method to Derive a Confidence Interval
All the intervals in this chapter come from one idea.
A pivotal quantity (pivot) is a function $g(X_1,\dots,X_n;\theta)$ of the sample and the unknown parameter whose distribution does not depend on $\theta$ (or on any other unknown parameter).
Recipe:
Find a pivot $g$ for $\theta$ with a known distribution.
Find constants $a,b$ with $\Prob(a\le g\le b)=1-\alpha$.
Rearrange $a\le g(X;\theta)\le b$ into $L(X)\le\theta\le U(X)$.
Pivots used in this chapter:
$\mu$, $\sigma$ known: $g=(\bar{X}-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\sim\Normal(0,1)$.
$\mu$, $\sigma$ unknown: $T=(\bar{X}-\mu)/(S/\sqrt n)\sim t_{n-1}$.
$\sigma^2$: $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$.
A Large-Sample Confidence Interval for $\mu$

If the population is not normal (or not assumed so) but $n$ is large, the CLT gives $\bar{X}\approx\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$. If $\sigma$ is unknown, replacing it by $S$ costs little, because $S$ is close to $\sigma$ for large $n$.
If $n$ is large (say $n\ge40$), an approximate $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval for the mean $\mu$ of any population with finite variance is
\bar{x}-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\ \le\ \mu\ \le\ \bar{x}+z_{\alpha/2}\frac s{\sqrt n}.
Bootstrap Confidence Intervals (CD Only)
For statistics like the median or a correlation, no pivot with a known distribution exists. The bootstrap of Chapter 1 gives the percentile interval.
Generate $B$ bootstrap estimates $\hat\theta^*_1,\dots,\hat\theta^*_B$ by resampling the data with replacement, and sort them. A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ percentile interval is
\big[\ \hat\theta^*_{(\alpha/2)},\ \hat\theta^*_{(1-\alpha/2)}\ \big],
the $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$ sample quantiles of the bootstrap distribution. With $B=1000$ and $\alpha=0.05$, these are the $25$th and $975$th ordered values.

A second version, the bootstrap standard-error interval, is $\hat\theta\pm z_{\alpha/2}\se_{\mathrm{boot}}$. It is reasonable when the bootstrap distribution is roughly normal. The bootstrap needs no distributional assumption, but it needs a reasonably large and representative sample. See Chapter 13.

sections.title: Confidence Interval on the Mean of a Normal Distribution, Variance Unknown

blocks.x: The $t$ Distribution
If $\sigma$ is unknown, replacing it by $S$ changes the sampling distribution of the pivot.
If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ is a random sample from a normal distribution with mean $\mu$, then
T=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
About the $t$ density:
Bell-shaped and symmetric about $0$, like the standard normal, but with heavier tails. The shape depends on the degrees of freedom $k=n-1$.
As $k\to\infty$, $t_k\to\Normal(0,1)$.
$t_{\alpha,k}$ is the point with right-tail area $\alpha$. For example $t_{0.025,9}=2.262$ and $t_{0.025,\infty}=1.960$.
Development of the $t$ Distribution (CD Only)
Write
T=\frac{(\bar{X}-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)}{\sqrt{S^2/\sigma^2}}=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-1)}},\qquad Z\sim\Normal(0,1),\quad V=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1},

with $Z$ and $V$ independent. That is the definition of the $t$ distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. Chapter 11 (Theorem 11.12) proves the independence of $\bar{X}$ and $S^2$ and the $\chi^2$ law of $V$, and writes down the density of $t_k$.
The $t$ Confidence Interval on $\mu$
Use $\Prob(-t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\le T\le t_{\alpha/2,n-1})=1-\alpha$ and rearrange:
If $\bar{x}$ and $s$ are the mean and standard deviation of a random sample from a normal distribution with unknown variance, a $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval on $\mu$ is
\bar{x}-t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac s{\sqrt n}\ \le\ \mu\ \le\ \bar{x}+t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac s{\sqrt n}.

One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bounds: upper $\mu\le\bar{x}+t_{\alpha,n-1}\,s/\sqrt n$; lower $\bar{x}-t_{\alpha,n-1}\,s/\sqrt n\le\mu$. They use $t_{\alpha,n-1}$, not $t_{\alpha/2,n-1}$, and give one limit only.
Ten measurements of the load at failure of a component: $\bar{x}=22.4$ kN, $s=3.0$ kN.
Each bound is tighter than the matching end of the two-sided interval.
Load at failure for $n=22$ specimens: $\bar{x}=13.71$, $s=3.55$. (The box plot and normal plot support normality.)
$21$ degrees of freedom, $t_{0.025,21}=2.080$.
The interval is fairly wide because the variability is large.

You cannot solve directly for the sample size that gives a target length. The length involves $s$ and $t_{\alpha/2,n-1}$, which depend on the data. Choose $n$ by trial and error from a prior guess of $\sigma$.

With $n=10$, the normal multiplier $1.96$ gives $22.4\pm1.86$. That is too short and covers $\mu$ less than $95\%$ of the time. The $t$ multiplier corrects for the extra uncertainty from estimating $\sigma$. The correction is large for $n<30$ and negligible for $n>100$.

The $t$ interval assumes a normal population. It is fairly robust to moderate non-normality for $n\ge15$ if the data are roughly symmetric. It is unreliable for small samples from skewed or heavy-tailed populations. Check with a normal probability plot.

sections.title: Confidence Interval on the Variance and Standard Deviation of a Normal Distribution

blocks.x: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be a random sample from $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with sample variance $S^2$. The pivot is
\chi^2=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
Let $\chi^2_{\alpha,k}$ be the point with right-tail area $\alpha$. Then $\Prob\big(\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\le(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\le\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}\big)=1-\alpha$.
A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval for $\sigma^2$ is
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}}\ \le\ \sigma^2\ \le\ \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}}.
Take square roots for an interval on $\sigma$.

One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bounds use $\alpha$ (not $\alpha/2$) and one limit: upper $\sigma^2\le(n-1)s^2/\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-1}$; lower $\sigma^2\ge(n-1)s^2/\chi^2_{\alpha,n-1}$. The upper bound divides by the small chi-square point. The lower bound divides by the large one.
$n=20$ fill volumes, $s^2=0.0153$.
The $\chi^2$ distribution is skewed, so the interval is not symmetric about $s^2$. The point estimate lies closer to the lower limit.
Unlike the $t$ interval for the mean, this interval is very sensitive to non-normality, because the distribution of $S^2$ depends on the fourth moment. Use it only when normality is credible.

sections.title: A Large-Sample Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

blocks.x: Let $X$ be the number of successes in $n$ independent trials with success probability $p$, and $\hat{P}=X/n$. For large $n$, the normal approximation to the binomial gives $\hat{P}\approx\Normal\big(p,\ p(1-p)/n\big)$. Replace $p$ in the variance by $\hat{p}$:
If $\hat{p}$ is the proportion of successes in a random sample of size $n$, an approximate $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval for $p$ is
\hat{p}-z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}n}\ \le\ p\ \le\ \hat{p}+z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}n}.
The approximation is acceptable when $n\hat{p}$ and $n(1-\hat{p})$ are both at least about $5$ to $10$.
One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bounds use $z_\alpha$ and one limit: $p\le\hat{p}+z_\alpha\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$ (upper), $\hat{p}-z_\alpha\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\le p$ (lower).
Among $n=85$ automobile crankshaft bearings, $10$ have rough surfaces. $\hat{p}=10/85=0.1176$.
To be $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confident that the error $\abs{\hat{p}-p}$ is at most $E$, use
n=\left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}}E\right)^2p(1-p).
Since $p$ is unknown, use a preliminary estimate, or the worst case $p=0.5$ (which maximises $p(1-p)=0.25$). That gives $n=0.25\,(z_{\alpha/2}/E)^2$.
A poll with a $\pm3\%$ margin at $95\%$ confidence and no prior information needs $n=0.25(1.96/0.03)^2=1067.1$, so $n=1068$.
The interval of Theorem 2.18 (the Wald interval) can have poor coverage when $p$ is near $0$ or $1$, or $n$ is small. Two better options:
The Wilson score interval: solve $\abs{\hat{p}-p}\le z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ for $p$ exactly, instead of plugging in $\hat{p}$.
The “add two successes and two failures” adjustment: use $\tilde{p}=(x+2)/(n+4)$ in the formula above.
Both have much better coverage. For $x=0$ successes, the $95\%$ upper bound is about $3/n$ (the “rule of three”).

sections.title: A Prediction Interval for a Future Observation

blocks.x: A confidence interval is about a fixed parameter. Often we want a range for the next individual value $X_{n+1}$, drawn from the same population.
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be a random sample from $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and $X_{n+1}$ an independent future observation. A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ prediction interval for $X_{n+1}$ is
\bar{x}-t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\,s\sqrt{1+\frac1n}\ \le\ X_{n+1}\ \le\ \bar{x}+t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\,s\sqrt{1+\frac1n}.
$X_{n+1}-\bar{X}$ is normal with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2+\sigma^2/n=\sigma^2(1+1/n)$, because the new observation is independent of $\bar{X}$. So
\frac{X_{n+1}-\bar{X}}{S\sqrt{1+1/n}}=\frac{(X_{n+1}-\bar{X})/(\sigma\sqrt{1+1/n})}{\sqrt{S^2/\sigma^2}}\sim t_{n-1},
and the interval follows as in Theorem 2.13.

Continue Example 2.14 ($n=10$, $\bar{x}=22.4$, $s=3.0$). The $95\%$ prediction interval for the next component is $22.4\pm2.262\cdot3.0\sqrt{1.1}=22.4\pm7.12$, that is $15.3$ to $29.5$. The confidence interval for $\mu$, $20.25$ to $24.55$, is much narrower.

As $n\to\infty$, the prediction interval tends to $\mu\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma$. It does not shrink to zero: no amount of data removes the variability of a single future value. The confidence interval shrinks to a point.

For a twenty-third specimen, the $95\%$ prediction interval is $13.71\pm2.080(3.55)\sqrt{1+1/22}=13.71\pm7.55$, that is $6.16$ to $21.26$. This is much longer than the interval $(12.14,\,15.28)$ for the mean. There is always uncertainty about the next observation, even when $\mu$ is known.

sections.title: Tolerance Intervals for a Normal Distribution

blocks.x: A tolerance interval aims to capture a stated proportion of the whole population, with a stated confidence that it really does.
A tolerance interval for capturing at least $100\gamma\%$ of the values of a normal distribution with confidence level $100(1-\alpha)\%$ is
\bar{x}-k\,s\ \le\ x\ \le\ \bar{x}+k\,s.

The constant $k=k(n,\gamma,\alpha)$ comes from tables or software. It is chosen so that, over repeated samples, a proportion $1-\alpha$ of such intervals contain at least a proportion $\gamma$ of the population.
A good approximation for the two-sided factor (Howe’s formula) is
k\approx z_{(1+\gamma)/2}\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)\,(1+1/n)}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-1}}},
where $\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-1}$ is the point with left tail area $\alpha$ (right-tail area $1-\alpha$).
$k\approx1.96\sqrt{9(1.1)/3.325}=1.96\sqrt{2.977}=3.38$. The exact tabled value is $3.38$.
With $\bar{x}=22.4$, $s=3.0$: $22.4\pm3.38\cdot3.0$, that is $12.3$ to $32.5$. Wider than the prediction interval $15.3$ to $29.5$.

To include $90\%$ of the population with $95\%$ confidence for $n=22$, Table XI gives $k=2.264$. The interval is $\bar{x}\pm2.264s=\bar{x}\pm8.04$. With $\bar{x}=13.71$ this is $(5.67,\,21.75)$. The width, $16.08$, is what matters.

As $n\to\infty$, $k$ approaches $z_{0.05}=1.645$ for a $90\%$ two-sided tolerance interval. A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ prediction interval tends to a tolerance interval containing $100(1-\alpha)\%$ of the distribution.
If $\mu=600$ and $\sigma=30$ are known, $600\pm1.96(30)=(541.2,\,658.8)$ captures $95\%$ of the population.
With $\bar{x}$ and $s$ in place of $\mu,\sigma$, the plain interval $\bar{x}\pm1.96s$ is likely to contain less than $95\%$. That is why $1.96$ is replaced by the larger factor $k$.
Confidence interval: where is the population mean? Narrowest. Shrinks with $n$.
Prediction interval: where will the next single observation fall? Limit $\mu\pm z\sigma$.
Tolerance interval: what range covers $95\%$ of all units, with $95\%$ confidence that the claim is right? Widest. Limit $\mu\pm z_{(1+\gamma)/2}\sigma$ from above.
Quality engineers use tolerance intervals for specification limits and confidence intervals for process averages.

$\sigma$ known: $\bar{x}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$. Sample size $n=(z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/E)^2$. One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bounds: $\bar{x}+z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n$ (upper) or $\bar{x}-z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n$ (lower). One limit only, and $\alpha$ not $\alpha/2$. The end of a two-sided $95\%$ interval is a one-sided $97.5\%$ bound.
$\sigma$ unknown (normal data): $\bar{x}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}s/\sqrt n$. Large samples (any population): $\bar{x}\pm z_{\alpha/2}s/\sqrt n$.
Variance: $\dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}}\le\sigma^2\le\dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}}$. Sensitive to non-normality.
Proportion: $\hat{p}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$. Sample size $n=(z_{\alpha/2}/E)^2p(1-p)\le0.25(z_{\alpha/2}/E)^2$.
Prediction interval: $\bar{x}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}s\sqrt{1+1/n}$. Tolerance interval: $\bar{x}\pm ks$.
The confidence level is the long-run coverage of the procedure. It is not the probability that one computed interval contains $\mu$.

The tensile strength of a fiber is normal with $\sigma=2$ MPa. A sample of $9$ has mean $98.5$. Find $90\%$, $95\%$ and $99\%$ confidence intervals for $\mu$ and the sample size needed to estimate $\mu$ within $0.5$ MPa with $95\%$ confidence.
A $95\%$ confidence interval for a mean based on $n=25$ and known $\sigma$ has length $4$. What would its length be for $n=100$? For $99\%$ confidence with $n=25$?

Data on the time (minutes) for a chemical reaction: $\bar{x}=45.2$, $s=4.1$, $n=12$ from a normal population. Find the $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$, the $95\%$ upper confidence bound for $\mu$, and the $95\%$ confidence interval for $\sigma$.

In a survey, $x=216$ of $n=400$ respondents prefer product A. Find the $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion in the population. How large a sample would give a margin of error of $2\%$ with $99\%$ confidence?
Explain, with a short numerical example, why a $95\%$ prediction interval is wider than a $95\%$ confidence interval from the same data, and compute both for $n=15$, $\bar{x}=50$, $s=6$.
Use Howe’s formula to compute the tolerance factor $k$ for $n=20$, $\gamma=0.99$, confidence $0.95$ (use $z_{0.995}=2.576$ and $\chi^2_{0.95,19}=10.12$).
Show that the width of the large-sample confidence interval for a proportion is largest at $p=0.5$, and derive the sample size formula of Theorem 2.20.
Draw $B=1000$ bootstrap samples from the data $4.1,\ 5.3,\ 3.9,\ 6.2,\ 4.8,\ 5.5,\ 4.4$ and form a bootstrap percentile $95\%$ interval for the median. Compare it with the $t$ interval for the mean.
